claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by low lattice distortion.
A nearly equal distribution of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti produces minimal local atomic-size mismatch and strain fields.
Minimal lattice distortion facilitates dislocation glide in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Facilitated dislocation glide provides favorable plasticity and machinability at the expense of hardness and yield strength.
Changing CoCrFeNiTi to a non-equimolar composition containing approximately 10 at.% Al will increase atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Increased lattice distortion will enhance dislocation pinning and impede dislocation motion.
Enhanced dislocation pinning will increase hardness and yield strength.
The modified non-equimolar alloy will have lower ductility than equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
XRD peak broadening or TEM imaging will reveal greater lattice distortion in the modified alloy.
The observed increase in lattice distortion will correlate with increased hardness and yield strength and reduced ductility.
The starting equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy has a uniform polycrystalline, minimally segregated solid-solution microstructure.
The proposed comparison is restricted to room-temperature, quasi-static loading with processing controlled to suppress secondary phases.
The hypothesis applies only where precipitation and grain-boundary effects do not significantly influence the measured properties.

contradictions.description: The intervention tests an explicitly non-equimolar Al-containing variant, whereas the boundary states that the hypothesis applies to equimolar or near-equimolar alloy conditions; it is unclear whether the proposed modified alloy remains inside the stated scope.
The conditions limit deformation to yield, but the boundary permits moderate plastic strain and the experiment proposes measuring ductility, which requires post-yield deformation.
